pos: n. (a place of instruction; a gathering for teaching and learning)
etymology: Greek schole, originally leisure, hence time given to learning — a place set apart from ordinary labor for instruction.
biblical_def:
But when divers were hardened, and believed not, but spake evil of that way before the multitude, he departed from them, and separated the disciples, disputing daily in the school of one Tyrannus.

Paul's two years in Ephesus pivot on this move: shut out of the synagogue by hardened unbelief, he does not abandon public teaching but relocates it to a rented lecture hall, disputing daily with whoever will come. The school of Tyrannus was almost certainly a secular rhetorician's hall, used for ordinary instruction the rest of the day, and Paul's daily use of it for two years produced a result Luke records with evident wonder: all they which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus. The word school names no special sanctity in the building itself; it was simply the ordinary civic infrastructure of learning, repurposed by daily, patient teaching into the engine of a region's evangelization.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SCHOLE (Gr.): a place of instruction; an institution or hall where students assemble to be taught.
webster_full: SCHOOL, n. A place or house in which persons are instructed in arts, science, or any branch of learning.
Used of a secular lecture hall rented for daily teaching, not a synagogue or temple.
Here identified by the name of its evident owner or proprietor, Tyrannus.
The setting for two years of Paul's daily disputations in Ephesus.
Ordinary civic space repurposed for the steady spread of the gospel.
scriptures: Act 19:9
But when divers were hardened, and believed not, but spake evil of that way before the multitude, he departed from them, and separated the disciples, disputing daily in the school of one Tyrannus.
corruption_summary: A sacred/secular divide that treats only church buildings as fit venues for gospel teaching misses Acts 19:9's example: Paul's most fruitful sustained ministry happened in a rented secular lecture hall, used daily for two years.
corruption_paragraphs: It is tempting to assume effective gospel teaching requires a consecrated space, but Luke records the opposite: shut out of the synagogue, Paul simply rents the ordinary infrastructure of a pagan city's education system and uses it daily.

The corrective is to see the school of Tyrannus as a model of patient, unglamorous means — the same hired room used by other teachers before and after Paul — producing extraordinary reach not because the venue was special but because the teaching was daily, public, and faithful for two full years.
roots_summary: Greek scholei, dative of schole, leisure or a place where leisure is spent in disputation — the ordinary Greek word for a lecture hall, carrying no religious connotation.
roots_lines: School here names an ordinary, secular lecture hall.
Paul is shut out of the synagogue before relocating there.
Two years of daily teaching follow from this single pivot.
The result is that all Asia hears the word of the Lord.
Ordinary civic space becomes the engine of regional evangelization.
usage: Disputing daily in the school of one Tyrannus — ordinary space, extraordinary fruit.
Two years of patient, public teaching follow.
All they which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus.

pos: n. (a person held in bondage as property; one deprived of liberty and owned by another)
etymology: Medieval Latin sclavus, originally Slav, from the mass enslavement of Slavic peoples in the early medieval period — a person wholly owned by another.
biblical_def:
Is Israel a servant? is he a homeborn slave? why is he spoiled?

Jeremiah's rhetorical question carries real bite: Israel is not a slave captured in war or purchased from a foreign market, but a homeborn slave, a son of the house treated as chattel in his own father's dwelling. The question why is he spoiled demands an answer the rest of the chapter supplies — covenant unfaithfulness, not an enemy's superior strength, has reduced a favored son to a plundered slave's condition. The word exposes the self-inflicted nature of Israel's calamity: no foreign power could have done to the covenant people what their own idolatry had already done, treating a son's inheritance as expendable as a slave's.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SLAVE: a person who is wholly subject to the will of another; one who has lost the power of self-direction, owned as property.
webster_full: SLAVE, n. A person who is held in bondage to another; one who has no freedom of action.
HOMEBORN SLAVE, a servant born in the master's own house, as distinct from a purchased or captured slave.
Used by Jeremiah as a rhetorical contrast to Israel's true status as a son.
Names a self-inflicted degradation, not an external conquest alone.
The question why is he spoiled points to covenant unfaithfulness as the true cause.
scriptures: Jer 2:14
Is Israel a servant? is he a homeborn slave? why is he spoiled?
corruption_summary: Jeremiah's question is not about the institution of slavery itself but about covenant unfaithfulness reducing a son to a condition beneath his birthright — a point easy to lose if the word is read only through modern debates about historical slavery.
corruption_paragraphs: Read in isolation, slave invites the reader to import contemporary debates the verse itself is not addressing. Jeremiah's concern is covenantal, not a commentary on ancient labor systems: Israel's sonship, not servitude generally, is the category being violated.

The corrective is to follow Jeremiah's own argument: a people adopted as sons (Exo 4:22, Hos 11:1) have been plundered as though they were property, because they abandoned the God who gave them their standing. The tragedy is self-inflicted, the result of idolatry, not an accident of history.
roots_summary: Hebrew yelid bayith, literally born of the house, the technical term for a servant born within a household rather than purchased — contrasted here with Israel's actual status as an adopted son.
roots_lines: Slave here names a status Israel should never have fallen into.
Jeremiah contrasts homeborn slave with Israel's true sonship.
The question why is he spoiled demands a covenantal, not military, answer.
Idolatry, not foreign strength, produced Israel's plundered condition.
The tragedy is self-inflicted, a son treated as chattel by his own unfaithfulness.
usage: Is Israel a servant? is he a homeborn slave? — a rhetorical contrast with true sonship.
Why is he spoiled? — demanding a covenantal, not merely political, answer.
Idolatry reduced a son's inheritance to a slave's plundered condition.

pos: n. (a female child; a young woman, here sold cheaply as an act of casual cruelty)
etymology: Middle English gyrle, of uncertain origin, originally a child of either sex before narrowing to a female child.
biblical_def:
And they have cast lots for my people; and have given a boy for an harlot, and sold a girl for wine, that they might drink.

Joel's indictment of Tyre, Sidon, and the Philistine coasts is almost unbearable in its specificity: conquered Israelite children, a boy and a girl, traded away as casual currency — one for a prostitute's wage, the other for a cup of wine. The word girl in this verse names not childhood innocence celebrated but childhood innocence priced at nothing, a single drink's worth, by captors who valued God's covenant people exactly as much as their appetites did. The verse functions as evidence in the Lord's lawsuit against the nations in Joel 3, and the casual cruelty it records — children as small change for pleasure — is precisely what calls down the valley of decision that follows.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from GIRL: a female child; a young female, applied here to a captive child sold in commerce.
webster_full: GIRL, n. A female child; a young woman, especially one not yet grown.
Used of a captive Israelite child, not a term of general description.
Paired with boy in the same verse, both sold for trivial payment.
Part of Joel's specific evidence against Tyre, Sidon, and Philistia.
Names the casual cruelty of treating covenant children as commerce.
scriptures: Joe 3:3
And they have cast lots for my people; and have given a boy for an harlot, and sold a girl for wine, that they might drink.
corruption_summary: Modern readers can pass quickly over this verse as ancient-world background detail, missing that Joel records it as specific, named evidence in God's lawsuit against the nations — the casual trading of children is itself the indictment.
corruption_paragraphs: It would be easy to treat a sold a girl for wine as incidental color in an ancient oracle against foreign nations, rather than as the precise charge being leveled. Joel names it as evidence, not atmosphere.

The corrective is to let the specificity stand: God's judgment in the following verses (the valley of Jehoshaphat, the valley of decision) is provoked exactly by this kind of casual cruelty toward the vulnerable, and the verse stands as a permanent reminder that how a nation treats its captive children is never beneath God's notice.
roots_summary: Hebrew yalda, a female child, paired with yeled, male child, in the same verse — the ordinary Hebrew terms for children, made devastating by the trivial price attached to them.
roots_lines: Girl here names a captive Israelite child, not a general term.
The verse pairs a boy and a girl, both sold for trivial payment.
This is specific, named evidence in the Lord's lawsuit against the nations.
The casual cruelty of the trade is itself the charge being leveled.
God's judgment in the following verses responds directly to this cruelty.
usage: Given a boy for an harlot, and sold a girl for wine — children as casual currency.
Named specifically as evidence against Tyre, Sidon, and Philistia.
The valley of decision follows directly from crimes exactly like this one.

pos: n. (land cultivated for produce; an estate devoted to agriculture)
etymology: Latin firma, a fixed payment or lease, via Old French ferme — land held under a fixed arrangement, later generalized to cultivated land itself.
biblical_def:
But they made light of it, and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise.

In the parable of the great supper, the invited guests do not refuse out of hostility but out of preoccupation: one to his farm, another to his merchandise, each choosing an ordinary, legitimate concern over the king's invitation. The farm is not condemned as sinful in itself; it is condemned as the thing chosen instead of the feast, made light of being the real crime, not farming being one. The parable's force depends on the ordinariness of the excuse — Christ is not warning against wicked distractions but against good, lawful ones allowed to outrank the gospel call, a danger far more common and far harder to detect than open rebellion.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from FARM: land let or held for cultivation; an estate devoted to the raising of crops or livestock.
webster_full: FARM, n. A tract of land appropriated to cultivation, held for the raising of crops.
Used in the parable of the great supper as one of two excuses offered.
Not condemned as sinful in itself; condemned as a competing priority.
Represents an ordinary, lawful occupation allowed to outrank the gospel call.
Paired with merchandise as the second excuse in the same verse.
scriptures: Mat 22:5
But they made light of it, and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise:
corruption_summary: A reading that assumes the invited guests must have had sinister reasons for refusing misses the parable's sharper point: ordinary, lawful concerns like a farm are precisely what most effectively crowd out the gospel's claim.
corruption_paragraphs: It would be more comfortable if the refused guests had wicked excuses, but Christ names a farm and merchandise — legitimate work, not vice — as what made light of the king's invitation. The danger the parable warns of is ordinary, not exotic.

The corrective is to hear made light of as the operative phrase: the farm itself is not the sin, but the silent ranking of it above the feast is. Any lawful good, held in this order, becomes the very thing that excludes a person from the wedding.
roots_summary: Greek agron, a field or piece of land, the ordinary word for agricultural ground, paired with emporian, trade or merchandise, in Christ's parable.
roots_lines: Farm names a lawful, ordinary occupation, not a sinful one.
It is one of two excuses given for refusing the king's invitation.
Made light of it, not the farm itself, is the condemned act.
The parable warns against good things ranked above the gospel.
Ordinary preoccupation, not open rebellion, excludes these guests.
usage: One to his farm, another to his merchandise — lawful excuses, fatal priorities.
Made light of it names the sin, not the occupation itself.
A warning against good things allowed to outrank the gospel call.

pos: n. (an armed raid or incursion; here, a sudden hostile foray rather than a highway)
etymology: Old English rad, a riding, journey on horseback — narrowing in this KJV usage to a mounted raid, before later settling to mean a highway.
biblical_def:
And Achish said, Whither have ye made a road to day? And David said, Against the south of Judah, and against the south of the Jerahmeelites, and against the south of the Kenites.

This is not the modern sense of road at all — Achish is asking David where he has conducted a raid, and David's answer is a calculated deception, naming targets to the south of Judah while actually having attacked Israel's enemies elsewhere, deliberately misleading his Philistine patron about his true loyalties. The word captures a precarious season in David's life, hiding among the Philistines from Saul while still, secretly, protecting Judah's interests through raids he then lies about to maintain his cover. Scripture records the deception without commentary, leaving the reader to weigh David's survival tactics against the straightforward ninth-commandment standard the rest of the canon upholds.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from ROAD: an inroad; a sudden incursion of an armed force into an enemy's territory; a raid.
webster_full: ROAD, n. (archaic) An incursion; a sudden attack or raid made by an armed force.
Distinct from the modern sense of a highway, now the word's exclusive meaning.
Used of David's raids while living among the Philistines.
Paired with a deliberately misleading answer to Achish.
Records a morally complex episode without explicit narrative commentary.
scriptures: And Achish said, Whither have ye made a road to day? And David said, Against the south of Judah, and against the south of the Jerahmeelites, and against the south of the Kenites.
corruption_summary: Reading road in its modern sense of a highway erases the verse's actual content entirely; recovering the archaic meaning is necessary before the moral question the episode raises can even be seen.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of its own — the risk here is linguistic drift rather than doctrinal pressure, since the word's modern meaning has nothing to do with its biblical use.

The principle worth recovering, once the archaic sense is restored, is Scripture's habit of recording its heroes' failures without excusing them: David's deception of Achish sits in the text unresolved, part of the full honesty of biblical narrative about even its most favored figures.
roots_summary: Hebrew pashat, to strip, spread out, used idiomatically of a raiding incursion that strips a territory of its goods — rendered road in the archaic English sense of a mounted foray.
roots_lines: Road here means an armed raid, not a highway.
Achish asks David where his raiding has taken him.
David answers with a deliberately misleading report.
The episode belongs to David's precarious time among the Philistines.
Scripture records the deception without excusing it.
usage: Whither have ye made a road to day — an archaic sense now entirely obsolete.
David's answer deliberately misleads his Philistine patron.
The episode is recorded candidly, without narrative excuse.

pos: n. (a structure of rungs for climbing; in Scripture, the figure of connection between heaven and earth)
etymology: Old English hlaeder, a stepped frame for ascending — the only occurrence of the word in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def:
And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it.

Jacob's ladder is the only ladder in the whole of Scripture, and its singular appearance carries enormous weight. A fugitive, alone, having just stolen his brother's blessing by deceit, sees a structure joining earth to heaven with angels in constant traffic upon it — and wakes to say surely the LORD is in this place, and I knew it not. Christ himself claims this image for his own identity in John 1:51, telling Nathanael that he will see heaven open and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man. The ladder is therefore not a static picture of access to God in general but a specific, Christ-shaped promise: he himself is the connection between heaven and earth that Jacob glimpsed only in a dream.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from LADDER: a frame with rungs for ascending or descending; figuratively, a means of rising from one state to another.
webster_full: LADDER, n. A frame of wood or other material, with steps or rounds, by which persons ascend and descend.
The only occurrence of the word in the Authorized Version.
Appears in Jacob's dream at Bethel, connecting earth to heaven.
Claimed by Christ in John 1:51 as a figure of himself.
Names the connection between God and man, not a general religious aspiration.
scriptures: And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it.
corruption_summary: A spiritualized reading that treats Jacob's ladder as a generic metaphor for climbing toward God by effort inverts the vision entirely: the ladder descends to a fugitive who has done nothing to deserve it, and Christ later claims it as himself, not as a program of ascent.
corruption_paragraphs: Self-help religion loves the image of a ladder to heaven, reading it as a program of ascent through effort or merit. The text records the opposite movement: God comes down to an undeserving fugitive while he sleeps, with no ladder-climbing required of Jacob at all.

The corrective is Christ's own interpretation in John 1:51: he is the ladder, the one mediator joining heaven and earth, so that access to God was never a matter of human ascent but of the Son of Man's own person connecting what sin had separated.
roots_summary: Hebrew sullam, found only here in the entire Old Testament, from a root meaning to raise or cast up — a genuine hapax legomenon describing a staircase or ramp-like structure.
roots_lines: Ladder occurs only once in Scripture, in Jacob's dream.
It connects earth to heaven with angels in constant traffic.
Jacob is a fugitive and deceiver, not a man ascending by merit.
Christ claims the image for himself in John 1:51.
Access to God is Christ's gift, not a program of human climbing.
usage: A ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven.
The angels of God ascending and descending on it.
Christ claims this image as his own identity in John 1:51.

pos: n. (fragrant wood; used only in the compound lign aloes, a prized aromatic timber)
etymology: French ligne, from Latin lignum, wood — preserved in the Authorized Version only within the single compound term.
biblical_def:
As the valleys are they spread forth, as gardens by the river's side, as the trees of lign aloes which the LORD hath planted, and as cedar trees beside the waters.

Balaam, hired to curse Israel, finds himself instead compelled to bless, and the images he reaches for are of flourishing, fragrant, divinely-planted abundance: valleys, riverside gardens, lign aloes, cedars beside the waters. The word lign survives in English only in this fossilized compound, naming a rare and costly aromatic wood imported from the East, used elsewhere in Scripture for embalming spices and as a figure of the bride's fragrance in Song of Solomon. Balaam's forced blessing pictures Israel not merely as prosperous but as deliberately, lavishly planted by the LORD himself — a people whose flourishing a hired curse-speaker is powerless to prevent because its source lies entirely outside his control.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from LIGNUM (L.): wood; preserved in English only in the compound lign aloes, a precious aromatic timber.
webster_full: LIGNUM, n. (L.) Wood; the material substance of a tree's trunk and branches.
LIGN ALOES, a fragrant Eastern wood, highly prized for its scent.
The word lign survives in English only within this single compound.
Used by Balaam as an image of Israel's divinely-planted flourishing.
Elsewhere associated with embalming spices and bridal fragrance.
scriptures: Num 24:6
As the valleys are they spread forth, as gardens by the river's side, as the trees of lign aloes which the LORD hath planted, and as cedar trees beside the waters.
corruption_summary: The rarity of the word lign in modern English leaves this image easy to pass over, but it anchors Balaam's prophecy in a specific, costly, deliberately-planted fragrance rather than vague prosperity.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Lign is a fossil word, not a term under cultural pressure, and the task is recovery rather than correction.

The principle worth recovering is the specificity of Balaam's blessing: which the LORD hath planted ties Israel's flourishing directly to God's own deliberate act, not to chance fertility, making the hired prophet's forced words a testimony against his own commission to curse.
roots_summary: Hebrew ahalim, aloes, paired loosely with the French-derived lign in English translation to specify the wood rather than the plant generally — the same Hebrew term appears in Psalm 45 and Song of Solomon.
roots_lines: Lign survives in English only in this one compound term.
Balaam is hired to curse Israel but is compelled to bless.
The images are of deliberate, divinely-planted abundance.
Lign aloes names a rare, costly, fragrant Eastern wood.
Israel's flourishing is attributed directly to the LORD's own planting.
usage: As the trees of lign aloes which the LORD hath planted.
Part of Balaam's forced blessing rather than his intended curse.
Flourishing attributed to God's deliberate act, not chance.

pos: n. (a Hebrew dry and liquid measure, equal to one homer, about sixty-two gallons)
etymology: Hebrew kor, a large measure, possibly related to a word for a round vessel or heap — the largest standard unit of measure in the Old Testament.
biblical_def:
Concerning the ordinance of oil, the bath of oil, ye shall offer the tenth part of a bath out of the cor, which is an homer of ten baths; for ten baths are an homer: for ten baths are an homer.

Ezekiel's temple vision descends, in this chapter, from soaring eschatology to exact administrative detail, and the cor sits at the center of that detail: the largest standard measure, equal to an homer, divided here into tenths for a precisely regulated oil offering. The specificity is the point. A vision as vast as a restored temple and a renewed land is not permitted to float free of concrete, checkable arithmetic — ten baths to the cor, a tenth of a bath required — because worship of the holy God has never been a matter of vague sincerity alone. The cor anchors transcendent vision to exact, honest measure.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from COR (Heb.): a Hebrew measure of capacity, the largest in use, equal to the homer, about sixty-two gallons.
webster_full: COR, n. A Hebrew measure, the same as the homer, used for both dry and liquid commodities.
Equal to ten baths, the standard liquid subdivision.
Used in Ezekiel's temple vision to regulate a precise oil offering.
The largest standard unit of measure named in the Old Testament.
Anchors a vast prophetic vision to exact, checkable arithmetic.
scriptures: Concerning the ordinance of oil, the bath of oil, ye shall offer the tenth part of a bath out of the cor, which is an homer of ten baths; for ten baths are an homer:
corruption_summary: Modern spirituality often treats precise, measured obedience as legalistic compared to sincere feeling, but Ezekiel's vision embeds exact measure — the cor, the bath, the tenth part — at the very center of restored, Spirit-filled worship.
corruption_paragraphs: It is tempting to read the measurement-heavy chapters of Ezekiel's temple vision as a dry appendix to the glorious vision that opens the book, but the text itself makes no such distinction: the glory of the LORD filling the house (Eze 43:5) and the exact arithmetic of the cor sit in the same prophetic unit.

The corrective is to recover the honoring of God in exact measure as itself an act of worship, not its opposite: a people who shortchange the tenth part of a bath while claiming sincere devotion have not actually honored the vision they claim to be inspired by.
roots_summary: Hebrew kor, used elsewhere of the large measures received and distributed in Solomon's and later administrations (1Ki 4:22, 2Ch 2:10), the standard bulk unit for grain and oil.
roots_lines: Cor names the largest standard measure in the Old Testament.
It equals an homer, divided into ten baths.
Ezekiel regulates a precise tenth-part oil offering from it.
Exact measure sits inside, not apart from, a transcendent vision.
Honoring God in precise arithmetic is itself an act of worship.
usage: The tenth part of a bath out of the cor — exact, regulated offering.
An homer of ten baths — the standard measure explained.
Precise measure embedded in a vision of restored worship.

pos: n. (a broken fragment of pottery; a shard)
etymology: Old English sceard, a fragment, gap, or notch — a piece broken from a larger earthen vessel, worthless in itself.
biblical_def:
And he shall break it as the breaking of the potters' vessel that is broken in pieces; he shall not spare: so that there shall not be found in the bursting of it a sherd to take fire from the hearth, or to take water withal out of the pit.

Isaiah's image of judgment on Judah's misplaced trust is total: not a cracked vessel repaired, but a potter's vessel shattered so completely that not one sherd remains large enough for the most menial household use — scooping a coal or dipping water. Even a sherd, the least valuable fragment imaginable, is denied the people under judgment. The specificity is the force of the warning: this is not partial discipline that leaves something useful behind, but a judgment as thorough as a vessel smashed past the point of any remaining utility, a fitting consequence for trust placed in Egypt's help rather than in the Holy One of Israel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SHERD (variant of SHARD): a broken piece of an earthen vessel; a potsherd.
webster_full: SHERD, n. A fragment of a broken earthen vessel; a shard.
The least valuable remnant of a pot, useful only for the most menial tasks.
Used by Isaiah as the measure of total, unsparing judgment.
Denied entirely to those under judgment, even for scooping a coal.
Follows directly from Judah's trust in Egypt rather than in the LORD.
scriptures: And he shall break it as the breaking of the potters' vessel that is broken in pieces; he shall not spare: so that there shall not be found in the bursting of it a sherd to take fire from the hearth, or to take water withal out of the pit.
corruption_summary: A therapeutic reading of divine discipline expects God's judgment to always leave something useful and redeemable behind, but Isaiah 30:14 pictures a judgment so total that not even a sherd, the least valuable fragment, survives.
corruption_paragraphs: It is comforting to assume judgment always leaves a remnant of practical use, a silver lining scaled to the severity of the discipline. Isaiah's image denies exactly that comfort: he shall not spare, and not a sherd remains for even the humblest task.

The corrective is to let the totality of the image stand as a warning proportioned to the sin: trust misplaced in a foreign power instead of the Holy One of Israel (the chapter's repeated charge) invites a judgment as complete as the trust was total. The sherd's absence is the point, not an oversight to be softened.
roots_summary: Hebrew cheres, broken pottery or earthenware, the same root behind potsherd and the word for clay itself, tying the image of total breakage to humanity's own origin from the dust.
roots_lines: Sherd names the least valuable fragment of a shattered vessel.
Isaiah pictures a judgment too total to leave even this behind.
The image follows Judah's trust in Egypt over the LORD.
He shall not spare signals unsparing, not partial, discipline.
The totality of the image is the sermon's point, not an excess of rhetoric.
usage: Not a sherd to take fire from the hearth — total, unsparing judgment.
Nor to take water withal out of the pit — no remaining use left at all.
A fitting consequence for trust misplaced in Egypt rather than the LORD.

pos: n. plural (wreaths of flowers or leaves, used in pagan religious ceremony)
etymology: Old French garlande, of uncertain further origin — a woven wreath used to crown sacrificial animals or idols in ancient worship.
biblical_def:
Then the priest of Jupiter, which was before their city, brought oxen and garlands unto the gates, and would have done sacrifice with the people.

Having just healed a man lame from birth, Paul and Barnabas are mistaken for gods descended to earth, and the priest of Jupiter prepares full pagan sacrificial honors — oxen for slaughter, garlands for crowning the victims or the supposed gods themselves. The apostles' horrified response, rending their clothes and running in among the people, shows the gospel's sharpest line: not indifference to how people worship, but violent refusal to receive worship due to God alone. Garlands here names the trappings of a religious impulse Scripture takes seriously as dangerous precisely because it is sincere — these are not cynical idolaters but genuinely grateful people reaching for the only categories of gratitude their paganism supplies.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from GARLAND: a wreath of flowers or leaves, worn as an ornament or used to crown a sacrifice or victor.
webster_full: GARLAND, n. A wreath of flowers, leaves, or vines, worn or used for decoration.
GARLANDS, plural; here specifically used in pagan sacrificial ceremony.
Brought alongside oxen for a planned sacrifice to Paul and Barnabas.
Met with the apostles' horrified refusal, not polite acceptance.
Represents sincere but misdirected worship, dangerous precisely for its sincerity.
scriptures: Then the priest of Jupiter, which was before their city, brought oxen and garlands unto the gates, and would have done sacrifice with the people.
corruption_summary: A pluralistic instinct to receive any sincere religious gesture graciously misses the apostles' own example: they rend their clothes and run among the crowd rather than permit garlands and sacrifice to be offered to them, however sincerely meant.
corruption_paragraphs: It would be easy to read the Lystrans' garlands as touching, even flattering, evidence of openness to the miraculous. Paul and Barnabas treat it instead as a crisis requiring immediate, forceful correction — sincerity is not a substitute for truth.

The corrective is the apostles' own speech that follows: we also are men of like passions with you, redirecting the crowd's genuine religious energy away from themselves and toward the living God who made heaven and earth. Garlands offered to a creature, however sincerely, must be refused, not graciously received.
roots_summary: Greek stemmata, wreaths or fillets used in sacrificial ritual, worn by the priest, the victim, or hung at the temple gates — standard apparatus of Greco-Roman sacrifice.
roots_lines: Garlands were standard apparatus of pagan sacrificial ceremony.
The priest of Jupiter prepares to sacrifice to Paul and Barnabas.
The apostles refuse the worship forcefully, not politely.
Sincere but misdirected worship is treated as genuinely dangerous.
The crowd's religious energy is redirected toward the true God instead.
usage: Brought oxen and garlands unto the gates — full sacrificial preparation.
Would have done sacrifice with the people — sincere, misdirected worship.
Met with the apostles' horrified and immediate refusal.
